title: Saga Pattern
description: Learn how to manage distributed transactions without two-phase commit using the Saga pattern — choreography, orchestration, and compensating transactions.

segments.text: In a monolith, a database transaction can span multiple tables atomically. In microservices, that transaction now spans multiple services with separate databases. You can't just use a traditional transaction anymore. So how do you ensure consistency?

Two-phase commit, or 2PC, is the traditional answer: a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then tells them all to commit. But 2PC is slow, blocking, and if the coordinator crashes, all participants are stuck holding locks. It doesn't scale for microservices.

The Saga pattern breaks a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions. Each service performs its local transaction and publishes an event. The next service reacts and performs its step. If any step fails, compensating transactions undo the previous steps.

Imagine placing an order. Step one: Order service creates the order. Step two: Payment service charges the card. Step three: Inventory service reserves the items. Step four: Shipping service schedules delivery. Each step is a local transaction.

Now what if inventory reservation fails because an item is out of stock? We can't just rollback — the payment was already charged in a different database. Instead, we run compensating transactions: refund the payment, then cancel the order. Each undo is explicit.
segments.thought_prompt: What if the compensating transaction itself fails? How would you handle that?

segments.text: In choreography-based sagas, there's no central coordinator. Each service listens for events and reacts. Order service emits 'OrderCreated,' Payment service hears it and charges the card, emits 'PaymentCompleted,' Inventory service hears that and reserves items.

Choreography is decentralized and loosely coupled. But as the saga grows, it becomes hard to understand the full flow. With ten services, you're chasing events through a maze. Debugging is painful because no single place shows the complete picture.

In orchestration-based sagas, a central orchestrator controls the flow. It tells each service what to do and waits for responses. The full saga logic lives in one place, making it easy to understand, modify, and debug.

The trade-off with orchestration is coupling. The orchestrator knows about all participating services, creating a central point of knowledge. If the orchestrator goes down, sagas stall. And it can become a bottleneck under high load.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose choreography over orchestration? Think about team structure and complexity.

segments.text: Both approaches require idempotent operations. Network failures mean messages can be delivered more than once. If the payment service receives 'charge card' twice, it must not charge twice. Use idempotency keys to make every step safe to retry.

Sagas replace the simplicity of ACID transactions with eventual consistency and explicit compensation logic. It's more work, but it's the reality of distributed systems. Choose choreography for simple flows with few services, orchestration when the saga is complex and needs clear visibility.
